reasons: Has a test file with many example sentences.
I did not run those tests in this session, so passing status is not confirmed here.

terms.meaning: a rule for finding a piece of text, such as a number followed by a currency word
a standard three-letter currency code such as USD or EUR
a word such as million or billion that multiplies a number
a word such as about or up to that makes an amount an estimate or limit
a number style where a comma marks the decimal point, common in Europe

used_by: Not visible in this packet. The header says every tool reads amounts through this file.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Purpose and currency table import
sections.what: States what the parser is for and loads the list of currencies the project holds exchange rates for.
sections.why: The header states that whole sentences caused years to be read as amounts.
sections.watch_out: Only currencies in the table are accepted as three-letter codes written before an amount.

sections.name: MoneyMention
sections.title: Shape of one money find
sections.what: Defines the fields of one find: the text, its position, currency, multiplier, the low and high values, the millions equivalents, the range flag, and the qualifier.
sections.why: Likely reason: one standard record for every caller.
sections.watch_out: The low and high values are in the number as written, while the millions fields are converted. Use the matching pair.

sections.name: PREFIX, ISO_PREFIX
sections.title: Currency symbols and codes before an amount
sections.what: Lists the symbols and codes that can come before an amount, such as a dollar sign, euro sign, or three-letter code.
sections.why: Likely reason: maps the written forms to standard codes.
sections.watch_out: A bare dollar sign maps to USD with a question mark, meaning the country is unknown. Callers must not treat it as US dollars.

sections.name: SUFFIX
sections.title: Currency words after an amount
sections.what: Lists currency words that can follow an amount, such as dollars, euros, or pounds.
sections.why: Likely reason: the same job as the prefixes, for amounts written the other way round.
sections.watch_out: The bare dollars word is also marked as unknown country. Some Scandinavian names map to an empty code and are left unresolved.

sections.name: SCALE, Fmt
sections.title: Magnitude words and qualifier words
sections.what: Maps magnitude words such as billion, crore and lakh to a multiplier. Also defines the words that mark a physical measure, such as tonnes or megawatts, and the qualifier words such as about or up to.
sections.why: Likely reason: a magnitude word makes a number money, and a qualifier marks it as an estimate.
sections.watch_out: Short abbreviations such as m and k are only trusted when a currency is written next to them, as later rules enforce.

sections.name: toNumber
sections.title: Converting digits to a number
sections.what: Turns a digit string into a number, deciding whether commas and dots are thousands separators or decimal points.
sections.why: Likely reason: English and European number styles differ, so the same text can mean different values.
sections.watch_out: With no format given, the shape is guessed. A plain comma with one or two digits is read as a decimal. Pass the format when it is known.

sections.name: CANDIDATE, CANDIDATE_NATIVE
sections.title: Patterns for finding numbers
sections.what: Defines the patterns that find number-like text, with an optional range dash, in English style and in the other-language style.
sections.why: Likely reason: the other-language style is opt-in so that older imports keep reading the same way.
sections.watch_out: Changing these patterns changes which numbers every caller finds, so older results can shift.

sections.name: SCALE_NATIVE
sections.title: Magnitude words in other languages
sections.what: Lists magnitude words in other languages, such as milliard, miljoner and Mrd, with their multipliers.
sections.why: The comment states they are for source-language amounts and are opt-in only.
sections.watch_out: They are only used when the other-language flag is set.

sections.name: SUFFIX_NATIVE
sections.title: Currency words in other languages
sections.what: Lists currency words in other languages, such as euros, kronor, kroner and punta, and the currency each maps to.
sections.why: The comment states these are for source-language amounts.
sections.watch_out: Some words, such as kroner and kr, match several currencies at once, so the result is not a single code.

sections.name: findMoneyMentions, SingleAmount (part 1)
sections.title: Scanning text for money
sections.what: Scans the text for number patterns. For each one it reads the currency before it, the magnitude word after it, and skips years and numbers stuck to a word.
sections.why: The comments state that years, codes and glued words are not money.
sections.watch_out: Any change here alters results for every caller, so the tests are the guard.

sections.name: findMoneyMentions, SingleAmount: if
sections.title: Filtering out non-money numbers
sections.what: Reads any currency word after the number, drops counts, percentages and physical quantities, and records a qualifier word before the amount.
sections.why: The comments state that abbreviations only signal money next to a currency.
sections.watch_out: A plain number with no currency and no magnitude is discarded, so a bare figure is missed by design.

sections.name: singleAmount, clip
sections.title: Choosing one amount or refusing
sections.what: Returns the one amount in a value, or a reason for refusing: no amount, several different amounts, a range, a qualifier, or no magnitude below 100,000 units. Also includes a helper that shortens long text in reasons.
sections.why: The comment states that the function never guesses which amount is the cost.
sections.watch_out: Plain figures under 100,000 with no magnitude word are refused on purpose, which can surprise someone expecting a value.

summary: Finds money amounts in free text and reports one amount only when it is clearly stated.
purpose: Read cost figures from research sentences without mistaking years or counts for money.
why: The header states that taking the first number read the year 2019 as the amount, so an amount must have a currency or a magnitude word.
how: Scans the text for number patterns, reads a currency symbol or code before the number, reads a magnitude word and a currency word after it, skips non-money numbers, records a qualifier before it, and then either returns one amount or refuses with a reason.
inputs: Text, an optional number format (decimal comma or decimal point), and an optional flag for other-language amounts.
outputs: A list of money mentions, or one amount in millions with its currency, or a reason for refusing.
risks: Rules are word and pattern based, so unusual phrasing or currencies may be missed or misread. Amounts written with no currency and no magnitude word are never read.
debug: Find the sentence in money.test.ts. Read the reason text from singleAmount to see why it refused. Check the number format argument if decimal points or commas look wrong.
